anchorData: ANCHORING PHENOMENON (Eldoret posho mill, owner Mzee Kiplagat). Both containers are CLOSED (with lid) and made from exactly 30,800 cm2 of iron sheet (no waste, no overlap). Cylindrical drum: radius r = 35 cm (diameter 70 cm), height h = 105 cm. Total SA = 2πr² + 2πrh = 7,700 + 23,100 = 30,800 cm2. Volume = πr²h = 22/7 x 1,225 x 105 = 404,250 cm3 = 404.25 litres. Rectangular box (square base): 50 cm x 50 cm x 129 cm. Total SA = 2(50x50) + 4(50x129) = 5,000 + 25,800 = 30,800 cm2. Volume = 50 x 50 x 129 = 322,500 cm3 = 322.5 litres. Comparison: SAs are EQUAL (30,800 cm2); the drum holds 81,750 cm3 (81.75 litres) MORE than the box; 1 litre = 1,000 cm3; 1 m3 = 1,000 litres = 1,000,000 cm3. Both containers are about 1 m tall, so they look roughly the same size. SUPPORTING DATA (use π = 22/7 everywhere). L1 and L5 classroom prism models: rectangular prism 5 cm x 4 cm x 3 cm (SA 94 cm2, V 60 cm3); triangular prism with right-angled triangle ends 3-4-5 cm and length 10 cm (SA = 2x6 + 12x10 = 132 cm2, V = 6 x 10 = 60 cm3). L2 Pyramid roof (school hall/homestead): square base 6 m x 6 m, vertical height 4 m, slant height 5 m (since 3² + 4² = 5²); roof area = 4 x ½ x 6 x 5 = 60 m2; volume = ⅓ x 36 x 4 = 48 m3. Regular triangular pyramid (tetrahedron) model: all edges 6 cm, each face 9√3 ≈ 15.59 cm2, total SA ≈ 62.35 cm2. L3 Ice-cream cone: r = 3.5 cm, slant l = 12 cm, curved SA = 132 cm2. Conical tank top: r = 1.4 m, slant l = 2 m, curved SA = 22/7 x 1.4 x 2 = 8.8 m2 of sheet. Turkana water tank frustum: big cone r = 2.1 m, slant 3.5 m, height 2.8 m; removed small cone r = 1.05 m, slant 1.75 m, height 1.4 m; frustum: R = 2.1 m, r = 1.05 m, slant 1.75 m, height 1.4 m; curved SA = π(R+r)l = 22/7 x 3.15 x 1.75 = 17.325 m2 (check: 23.1 - 5.775 = 17.325). Frustum volume = 12.936 - 1.617 = 11.319 m3 = 11,319 litres. L4 Football: r = 10.5 cm, SA = 4πr² = 1,386 cm2, V = 4/3πr³ = 4,851 cm3. Nairobi packaging factory composite container: cylinder r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm with hemisphere on top (no lid between): SA = curved cylinder 440 + base 154 + hemisphere 308 = 902 cm2; volume = 1,540 + 718.67 (= 2/3 x 22/7 x 343 = 2,156/3 ≈ 718.67) ≈ 2,258.67 cm3. L6 matching cone/cylinder models: r = 7 cm, h = 12 cm; cylinder V = 1,848 cm3; cone V = 616 cm3 (a third; 3 cone-fuls fill the cylinder). L7 Water tank: cylinder r = 2.1 m, h = 4 m with hemispherical top, flat base; SA = wall 52.8 + base 13.86 + hemisphere 27.72 = 94.38 m2; V = 55.44 + 19.404 = 74.844 m3 = 74,844 litres. Rift Valley grain silo: cylinder r = 2.1 m, h = 6 m, cone roof height 2.8 m, slant 3.5 m; wall = 79.2 m2, roof = 23.1 m2, floor = 13.86 m2; total SA = 116.16 m2; volume = cylinder 83.16 + cone 12.936 = 96.096 m3. Do NOT invent other figures for the anchoring phenomenon.
characters: Mzee Kiplagat: owner of a posho mill in Eldoret, puzzled that equal sheet gives unequal grain capacity. Wanjiru: jua kali metalsmith in Eldoret who made both containers from 30,800 cm2 of sheet each; she measured, not guessed. The drum (cylinder, r 35 cm, h 105 cm) and the box (50 x 50 x 129 cm) are the two containers used by all lessons. Maasai manyatta and school hall roofs (Kajiado/Narok): pyramid and cone roof examples (L2, L3). Turkana water project: frustum-shaped raised tank (L3, L6). Nairobi packaging factory: makes cylinder-with-dome containers and cartons (L4). Footballs: used by learners from a school in Kisumu (L4, L6). Rift Valley (Nakuru/Uasin Gishu) cooperative: owns the grain silo (L7). Groups in L8 design a grain silo, water tank or cooking pot (sufuria) for a named community need. Careers: metal fabricator, civil engineer, architect, packaging engineer, quantity surveyor.
outcome: The drum and the box have the same total surface area (30,800 cm2) but different volumes: the drum holds 404,250 cm3 (404.25 litres) and the box 322,500 cm3 (322.5 litres), so the drum holds 81.75 litres more maize. Surface area measures the material covering a solid, while volume measures the space inside, and they are different quantities: for a fixed surface area, the shape (here the circular cross-section, which encloses more area for its perimeter than a square) determines capacity. A sphere is best of all, so artisans use mathematics to choose shapes (cylinders, domes, cones) and dimensions that give the largest capacity for the least sheet metal, balanced against practical needs like stacking and cost.
conventions: Use π = 22/7 in all calculations unless stated. Write area units as cm2, m2 and volume units as cm3, m3; 1 m3 = 1,000 litres; 1 litre = 1,000 cm3. Vertical (perpendicular) height = h; slant height = l (never call l 'height'); radius = r, frustum large radius = R, small radius = r. Total surface area (TSA) includes every face including bases/lids; curved (lateral) surface area excludes bases; always state which. Formulae: prism TSA = 2 x base area + perimeter of base x length; pyramid TSA = base area + sum of triangular face areas; cone curved SA = πrl, TSA = πr(r + l); frustum curved SA = π(R + r)l; sphere SA = 4πr²; hemisphere curved SA = 2πr²; prism/cylinder V = base area x h; pyramid/cone V = ⅓ x base area x h; sphere V = 4/3πr³; hemisphere V = 2/3πr³; frustum V = big cone - small cone. Words: 'net' = flat pattern of a solid; 'capacity' = volume of container in litres. 'Surface area' and 'volume' are never interchangeable. The 'drum' is the cylinder and the 'box' the rectangular container; both closed with lids. Always compare SA of containers before comparing volumes. DQB = Driving Question Board. Round only at the final step to 2 decimal places.
